clips.title: 5 JavaScript API Key Mistakes (and how to fix them)
clips.why: The pattern you already know from frontend work: the browser never holds the key, a small server of yours adds it on the way.
look: Where the key lives once the proxy exists, and what the browser code still knows.
That the proxy itself becomes a door: think about who is allowed to call it.
Which parts of the request the proxy passes on unchanged.
clips.after: Our gateway is that proxy for Claude, with one addition: it answers only callers that show a valid run token, so nobody else can spend our keys through it.

clips.title: MAC / HMAC - Message Authentication Code / Hash Bashed Message Authentication Codes
clips.why: A clear, short explanation of the fingerprint that makes a run token impossible to change: a hash mixed with a secret key.
look: Why a plain hash is not enough: anyone can compute it again after changing the message.
What the secret key adds: only someone who holds it can make a matching fingerprint.
That the receiver checks by computing the fingerprint again, with no list of valid messages.
clips.after: The gateway checks each run token exactly this way: it computes the HMAC of the claims with the signing key from Vault and compares, so it needs no database of tokens.

clips.title: LiteLLM Proxy Tutorial: Track Costs, Budgets, and Multi-Provider LLM Usage
clips.why: An open-source LLM gateway doing the same swap: apps get keys made by the proxy, the proxy holds the provider's real key, and spend is counted per key.
look: The virtual keys: passes made by the proxy, not keys from the model provider.
Spend tracked per virtual key, which is our cost per agent, ticket and run.
That LiteLLM can block a key that goes over its budget. Our gateway deliberately never does.
clips.after: Our run tokens are virtual keys that are made per run and expire. Unlike this setup, a run that spends a lot is never cut off at the gateway; the harness decides between turns.

practice.q: Which environment does the harness give the Claude session inside the VM?

options.text: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY set to the nova workload's key
options.why: That puts the real key on the machine, where any command the agent runs can read it.

options.text: ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL set to the gateway and ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN set to the run token
options.why: Every model call goes to our gateway with the run token as Authorization: Bearer, and the gateway adds the key.

options.text: ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL set to https://api.anthropic.com and ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN set to the run token
options.why: Anthropic has never seen our tokens and refuses them. The token only means something at our gateway.

practice.q: The gateway sends only these request headers on to Anthropic. Which header must never be in the list, because it carries the run token?
practice.hint: Claude Code puts ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN into it as Bearer <token>.
practice.why: The run token arrives in Authorization. Leaving that header out of the list means the token never leaves our network, and Anthropic only ever sees x-api-key.

practice.q: Put one model call from Nova's VM in order.
items: The harness sends POST /v1/messages to the gateway with Authorization: Bearer <run token>
The gateway checks the token's HMAC, its expiry and Nova's epoch
The gateway drops the token and adds x-api-key with the nova workload's key from Vault
The request goes on to api.anthropic.com with the same body
The answer streams back to the VM as it arrives, and the gateway counts only the usage numbers
practice.why: The only thing that changes on the way is the credential. A token that fails the check never gets past the second step.

practice.q: A Nova run token from Monday turns up in a log on Wednesday, and someone inside our network sends it to the gateway. Monday's run ended long ago. What stops the call?

options.why: The signature is still valid: nobody changed the claims. A signature proves who made the token, not that it is still alive.

options.text: The gateway remembers which runs have ended
options.why: The gateway keeps no list of tokens or runs. It checks everything from the token itself.

options.text: The exp claim: the gateway refuses a token after its expiry time
options.why: That is why the expiry check matters even with a good signature. Without it, a leaked token would work forever, like a key.

practice.q: In the middle of a long build, Anthropic answers 529 (overloaded). What does the gateway do?

options.text: Passes the 529 back with its retry-after header; the harness waits and tries again
options.why: The gateway touches only the credential. Retrying is the harness's job, and nothing in the gateway cuts the run short.

options.text: Turns it into a 401 so the run stops
options.why: That would tell the harness its token is bad, and it would stop a healthy run for a short outage.

options.text: Keeps retrying inside the gateway until Anthropic answers
options.why: The gateway holds no retry logic. Passing the answer back lets the harness wait the time Anthropic asked for.

practice.q: A confused session in Nova's VM adds its own header, x-jira: RH-9999, to every model call. The run token says jira: RH-1234. Which ticket does the gateway count the cost against?

options.text: RH-9999, because the header is newer than the token
options.why: The gateway never reads cost tags from headers, because the VM can set a header to anything.

options.text: RH-1234, because the tags come from the token's signed claims
options.why: The claims are signed, so the VM cannot change them. That makes the token the one source of truth for agent, ticket and run, even when the session is confused.

options.text: Neither: the gateway refuses the call with 401 because of the unknown header
options.why: An extra header is not a bad token. The gateway simply does not forward it, and the call goes through.
